findings.title: prisma is used but never imported — build-breaking error
findings.body: The newly added token-refresh block calls `await prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })` at lines 96–99, but the file's import list (lines 1–20) does not import `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. This is a compile-time TypeScript error (`Cannot find name 'prisma'`) and will fail the build/type-check for the whole app-store package.

findings.title: Zod safe-parse wrapper object is stored as the credential key, corrupting the credential
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the raw `schema.safeParse(...)` result, i.e. an object of the form `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. The code then does `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema); await prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, persisting the wrapper — not the parsed tokens — into `credential.key`. The next time a `GoogleCalendarService` is constructed, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` (line 75) fails because the stored value has shape `{success, data}` instead of the token shape, so every Google Calendar operation for that user throws after the first token refresh. Previously the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the data itself); the fix is to store `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data`.

findings.title: Sync-mode return type (raw fetch Response) is incompatible with several callers' expectations
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, but in non-sync mode it returns whatever the provider-specific `refreshFunction` returns — and callers rely on those provider shapes. Concretely: (1) `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 94 does `const token = res?.data` — a `Response` has no `.data`, so `token.access_token` throws a TypeError that is swallowed by the surrounding catch, meaning the access token is silently never refreshed in sync mode and Google calls fail with 401 once expired. (2) `hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts` lines 192–202 treat the return value as a HubspotToken: `expiryDate` becomes NaN, `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(undefined)` is called, and the `Response` object itself is serialized into `credential.key` in the DB, corrupting the credential. (3) `zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 217 and `zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 96 access `tokenInfo.data` (axios shape) — `Response.data` is undefined, so reading `.data.error`/assigning `.data.expiryDate` throws and refresh always fails in sync mode. Either `refreshOAuthTokens` must normalize the sync response (e.g. parse JSON and return it) or every call site must handle both shapes.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys are literal "[object Object]" and validate nothing about expiry
findings.body: The schema uses computed property names `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. `z.string()` returns a ZodString instance whose `toString()` yields `"[object Object]"`, so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() }` — the intended 'any numeric property is the expiry' validation never happens. Worse, zod strips unknown keys by default, so when credential sync is enabled the parsed `data` contains only `access_token`; `expires_in`/`expiry_date` are dropped. Downstream consequences: in `zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts` line 122, `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` becomes NaN and is persisted, after which `isTokenValid` (`NaN < Date.now()` is false) treats the token as valid forever, so Zoom stops refreshing and API calls fail once the synced token expires. In `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` the `expires_in`→absolute-timestamp transform is also skipped in sync mode (see separate finding).

findings.title: Credential ID is passed to refreshOAuthTokens where a user ID is expected
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)` sends its third argument to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Every other app passes `credential.userId`, but zoho-bigin passes `credentialId` (the credential row's primary key, from `refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey)`). With sync enabled, the self-hoster's endpoint receives `calcomUserId=<credential id>`, looks up the wrong (or no) user, and returns tokens for the wrong account or an error — so Bigin token refresh is broken/mis-attributed whenever credential sync is on.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token" and persisted
findings.body: When the (sync) response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers such as `zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts` (line 120: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`) and `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` then write this placeholder into `credential.key` in the database, overwriting the real OAuth refresh token. If credential sync is later disabled (or for apps like Salesforce that still hit the provider directly), the stored credential can never be refreshed again and the integration is permanently broken until the user reconnects.

findings.title: Sync mode skips the expires_in→absolute-expiry transform, causing a token refresh on every API call
findings.body: In non-sync mode, `refreshTokenResponseSchema` transforms `expires_in` (seconds) into an absolute epoch timestamp via `.transform()`. In sync mode, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` uses `minimumTokenResponseSchema`, which performs no transform and strips unknown keys, so `o365AuthCredentials` keeps its old, already-expired `expires_in` value. Since `getToken` decides to refresh based on `isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)`, every single `getToken()` call triggers another POST to the sync endpoint — one extra HTTP round-trip (plus a DB write) per calendar operation, and the stored `refresh_token` is also clobbered with the placeholder string.

findings.title: Webex refresh bypasses parseRefreshTokenResponse, so sync-mode responses always fail schema validation
findings.body: Unlike the other apps, the Webex adapter was wrapped with `refreshOAuthTokens` but still validates the result with the strict `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)` instead of `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. That schema requires `scope` to be the exact literal "spark:kms meeting:schedules_read meeting:schedules_write", `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Per the PR's own contract (comment in `refreshOAuthTokens`: 'The response should only contain the access token and expiry date'), the sync endpoint returns a minimal payload, so validation fails and every Webex token refresh rejects with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' whenever credential sync is enabled.

findings.title: Salesforce now refreshes the token on every service instantiation and ignores the credential-sync endpoint
findings.body: The new code in `getClient` unconditionally POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and writes to the DB every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed — previously jsforce lazily refreshed only on a 401. This adds an external HTTP call plus a DB write to every Salesforce calendar operation. Additionally, this is the only modified app that does not route through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so when credential syncing is the source of truth, the stored `refresh_token` may be the placeholder `"refresh_token"` (or absent), making this direct Salesforce refresh fail with invalid_grant and breaking the integration entirely.

findings.title: findFirst-then-create upsert has a race that creates duplicate credentials
findings.body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ userId, appId })` and then either updates or creates. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app (retries are typical for webhooks) can both observe no existing credential and both execute `prisma.credential.create`, leaving duplicate credential rows for the same user and app. Other parts of the codebase use `findFirst` when reading credentials, so duplicates silently shadow each other and can cause the wrong (stale) credential to be used. Since `(userId, appId)` is not unique in the schema, this should at least be serialized (e.g. transaction with locking, or a unique constraint) rather than a check-then-act.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with !== (non-constant-time comparison)
findings.body: The shared-secret check `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses a regular string comparison, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is susceptible to timing side-channel measurement of the secret. For a secret that gates writing arbitrary credentials into the database, `crypto.timingSafeEqual` (after length check) should be used. Additionally, `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throw unhandled exceptions, returning a stack-trace-bearing 500 instead of a 400.

findings.title: No tests for the credential-sync webhook or the sync-mode token refresh paths
findings.body: The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The new endpoint writes third-party credentials directly into the database and the modified refresh paths in ~10 app integrations (Google, Zoom, Office365, HubSpot, Zoho, Webex, Lark, Salesforce) now branch on `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` — several of which are broken in sync mode (shape mismatches, NaN expiry, wrapper object persisted). At minimum, tests covering the webhook (auth failure, create vs update, bad payload) and one representative sync-mode refresh per response-shape family (fetch Response vs SDK object vs axios) would have caught the regressions in this PR.
